subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: learning by building a tiny project [Action]
passage: Gargi had forty minutes a night after homework, and a laptop she shared with her father. She decided to build a quiz for her class's history test. She typed ten questions into a Python list. She learned what a for-loop was because she needed to go through the questions, and learned input() because she needed the answers. When the score wouldn't add up, she searched the error, found she had typed the number as text, and fixed it. On Friday her classmate Suraj tried the quiz, scored seven out of ten and asked, “Can you make one for geography?” By the next week a dozen classmates had copied the file to the school lab computers. It was untidy, and it worked.

qa.q: How many minutes did Gargi have each night?
How might Gargi have felt when the score would not add up?
qa.a: Frustrated and stuck at first, but she searched the error instead of giving up 🙂.

qa.q: What else could Gargi do to improve the quiz, and why?
qa.a: Ask classmates which questions confused them and add more, since real use shows what is needed.

qa.q: How does the quiz look to Suraj?
qa.a: Suraj gets a lively way to revise and asks for geography, so it feels useful instead of like another assignment.

grounding: A teen builds a quiz for classmates, learning only the loops, lists and input she needs, and ends with something friends use.

subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: learning by building a tiny project [Action]
passage:
Elizabeth's plan fit on one sticky note: ten questions, a score at the end, classmates can play. The science quiz club at her school in Pune met every Thursday, and Jahnavi, the club secretary, was tired of reading questions aloud from paper.
Elizabeth didn't start a course. At the small desk in the corner of the family flat, she opened a blank file and wrote what she needed first: a way to ask a question. She searched how to take input, tried it, and it worked. Storing ten questions meant lists, so she looked those up next. Repeating the asking needed a loop; that cost an evening of errors and one short explainer video.
By Wednesday night the quiz ran on the club laptop. On Thursday, Jahnavi played first, scored seven, and demanded a rematch. Four more members tried it before the bell.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth write on her sticky note?
qa.a: Ten questions, a score at the end, classmates can play.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth probably feel when the loop took an evening of errors, and what kept her going?
qa.a: She was likely frustrated, but the goal of a working quiz by Thursday kept her motivated enough to watch one explainer and fix it.

qa.q: What else could Elizabeth have done if the loop errors had lasted for days?
qa.a: She could post the code and the error on a learner forum or ask the computer teacher, since one specific question gets unstuck faster than more videos.

qa.q: How does the quiz look to Jahnavi on Thursday?
qa.a: For Jahnavi it is a relief from reading questions off paper, and fun enough that she wants to play again.

grounding: Shows a teen learning only input, lists and loops as her quiz needs them, looking things up when stuck, and ending with a quiz club members use.

subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: learning by building a tiny project [Action]
passage:
“Simran, try typing ‘delhi’ in small letters.”
“Okay... it says wrong! Madhuri, your quiz is lying.”
“I know. That's today's problem. Yesterday's was how to keep the questions in a list.”
“Why not just do a proper full course first?”
“Because I only need four things: asking, storing, repeating and checking. I learn each one when I hit it.”
Madhuri typed a search into the lab computer, read for a minute, and added one line. “There. Now it turns every answer into small letters before comparing.”
“Delhi... correct! Now mine: ‘plassey’.”
“Correct too.” Simran grinned at her. “Can you send it to the class group before Friday's history test?”
“Already did. Nine people played it last night, and someone's cousin asked for a maths version.”

qa.q: What does the new line Madhuri adds do?
qa.a: It turns every answer into small letters before comparing.

qa.q: Why is Madhuri so relaxed when the quiz marks the answer wrong?
qa.a: Madhuri feels unbothered and confident, because fixing one problem at a time is the plan and the bug is simply "today's problem" 🙂

qa.q: Which approach would suit Madhuri better if a feature needed something much harder, like saving high scores?
qa.a: Keep learning just that piece, but ask the computer teacher which topic to search first, so the search does not wander into unrelated lessons.

qa.q: How does the quiz look to Simran and the class before the history test?
qa.a: For them it is a quick, useful revision tool; nine people have already played it, which shows it meets a real need.

grounding: Shows a teen learning only the parts her history quiz needs, looking up each fix as she gets stuck, and ending with a quiz classmates actually use.
